speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry will then speak on energy costs, supply chains and support for businesses, as well as the Committee Against Profiteering.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members, namely, Mr Christopher de Souza, Dr Wan Rizal1, Mr Liang Eng Hwa2, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Darryl David3 and Mr Alex Yam4 have filed Questions for Oral and Written Answers scheduled for future Sittings on these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As today's Ministerial Statements will address these questions, I would invite these Members to seek clarifications on these issues after the Ministerial Statements, if need be.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If their questions are sufficiently addressed, it may not be necessary for them to proceed with the Questions for future Sittings.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, global prices were already rising last year, and there are a few reasons for this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Major economies like the US and the Eurozone have pursued expansionary macroeconomic policies and these were to stimulate their economies since the pandemic hit.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This contributed to a surge in demand, including for energy, especially after these economies began to ease up on their COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But supply was unable to catch up with demand.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, there were more unexpected gas production outages during this period.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The supply constraints were exacerbated by the under-investment in fossil fuel production over the past few years, due in part to the global push for greener sources of power.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But these renewable sources of power have not been able to scale up quickly enough.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There have also been continued supply chain pressures due to COVID-19, such as port congestion and freight capacity constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These pressures have impacted all industries, some more than others.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, several major advanced economies face labour tightness, which have driven up labour costs and these have, in turn, passed through to inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All of these factors led to a rise in inflation in the major economies last year.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Global energy supplies will remain tight, given that Russia is one of the world's largest oil and gas exporters.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For now, Russian gas is still flowing into Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Countries, such as Germany and Austria, which are highly reliant on Russian gas, are already putting in place their first phase of rationing of gas, in anticipation of a disruption of supplies from Russia.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The US is releasing a record amount of oil from its emergency reserves and exporting LNG to Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But this may not be sufficient to make up for the potential supply loss from Russia.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The tightness in the energy market will also have downstream impact on other related sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, many refineries in Germany rely exclusively on piped gas from Russia for their operations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the Russian gas supply is disrupted, these refineries will have to shut their operations and there will be adverse impact on the downstream production of chemical products, from plastics and fertilisers to fibres and solvents.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The war has impacted global food supplies, resulting in higher food prices.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Russia and Ukraine are major exporters of agricultural products, such as wheat, corn and barley, as well as fertilisers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, Ukraine is sometimes called the "bread basket of Europe".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the war, food exports from these countries will be significantly impacted.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Fertiliser shortages will also reduce crop yields elsewhere, resulting in a smaller harvest in the coming year.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a result, prices of a range of agricultural commodities, not just wheat and corn, are now at cyclical highs, pointing to potentially tight stocks this year.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides the two key areas of energy and food, production is affected in other areas too.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, Russia is a significant exporter of important industrial metals like palladium, used in catalytic converters for cars, and nickel, used in steel and batteries.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: About half the world's neon, which is used in the chip production process, is produced in Ukraine.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In short, the war has contributed to a further spike in inflation experienced around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Inflation in Germany and America has already risen to nearly 8%, the highest in 40 years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: No one can tell how the war in Ukraine will unfold.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We all hope that attempts to de-escalate are successful, and a diplomatic solution can be found at the negotiating table.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we must be prepared for a prolonged conflict, or even further escalation, which will cause further supply disruptions and additional inflationary pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides the war, there are other factors contributing to rising prices.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The global economy is continuing to grapple with supply chain issues due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The recent lockdowns in Chinese cities like Shenzhen and Shanghai have worsened strains in shipping and supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If there are continued periodic lockdowns in China or other major economies in the coming months, for example, to prevent the spread of a new and more dangerous variant, then we can expect further supply disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, both the pandemic-related disruptions and the Russian invasion of Ukraine have prompted companies to take supply chain risks more seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is renewed momentum to re-shore production, either back to the home countries of multinational corporations, or to more locations across different markets, so as to avoid single points of failure.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, the highly efficient, just-in-time global supply chain network is being reconfigured to account for once-unimaginable tail risks.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This can help make supply chains more resilient but will add to production and transport costs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the longer term, global warming and increased adverse weather events could affect agricultural productivity and reduce food production, putting upward pressure on prices.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over time, the global economy will also have to internalise the cost of carbon in our overall consumption, as part of the green transition.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, amidst this backdrop, the central banks of several major economies have shifted their position to take a stronger stance against inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England have raised interest rates to tackle inflation, with the European Central Bank expected to follow suit.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But central banks in these major economies also face a very difficult dilemma.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If they were to raise interest rates too sharply to tackle inflation, they will slow down economic activity or even trigger a recession.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the other hand, if they do not raise interest rates sufficiently, they will find it hard to anchor longer-term inflation expectations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They will then risk prices drifting persistently higher and becoming harder to control over time.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is why some economists have drawn analogies between the current situation and what happened in the 1970s.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, there was also excess demand, as the US had pursued expansionary policies to push for economic and employment growth.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When the oil crisis hit in 1973, the effect was immediate and dire.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Oil prices shot up and inflation rose sharply.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It took the US Federal Reserve many years to bring inflation under control and this was eventually achieved only at great cost to the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: History does not repeat itself but, as the saying goes, it often rhymes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: No doubt, the global economy today is very different from what it was in the 1970s and central banks and market institutions have also evolved greatly in sophistication since then.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the downside risks of higher inflation and slower growth for the global economy have increased significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If these downside risks were to materialise, they will have a major impact on Singapore as a small and open economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had earlier anticipated some of these risks and had taken prompt actions through both monetary and fiscal policies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Monetary policy will continue to do its part to ensure medium-term price stability.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS is watching closely the impact of geopolitical and pandemic-related shocks on the Singapore economy and inflation and will be putting out its monetary policy statement, as scheduled, later this month.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where fiscal policy is concerned, we had taken into account the risks in the global economy and rolled out an expansionary Budget this year.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had also implemented very comprehensive and substantial support packages to help households and businesses cope with higher prices.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members asked whether the Government will consider enhancing the support measures announced in the Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The measures in the Budget have just been announced and will be implemented soon.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will need time to allow these measures to take effect and feed through the economy before we monitor their impact, assess the overall situation and then consider what additional steps we might want to take.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Nevertheless, I understand the concerns that many households and businesses have about the current situation and have decided to take the following immediate actions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, where possible, I will bring forward the implementation of our Budget measures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is on top of the $100 disbursed four months ago in December last year and will help Singaporeans with their daily expenses.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Budget also included rebates for Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) and utility bills.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will disburse the first tranche of S&CC rebates and U-Save rebates to eligible households this month.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will address a key cost of living component which several Members have asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is the first tranche of the rebates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Most eligible businesses will be able to receive the grant by June.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The recent easing up of safe management measures (SMMs) should also provide some additional revenue support for local businesses, especially in the retail and F&B sectors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, we will provide more help for lower-income households, which will be more impacted during this period of higher prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Households which are already on ComCare SMTA can also have their assistance extended for at least another three months if they require further assistance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: SSOs will continue to exercise flexibility to provide those in need with financial assistance and support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This includes providing ComCare recipients with more cash assistance during this period to cope with inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The COVID-19 Recovery Grant is also in place until the end of this year and this will help lower- to middle-income households experiencing job losses or sustained income losses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And families who need help can also approach their Community Centres, or CCs, and the Self-Help Groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These schemes complement our national schemes, bringing more help closer to residents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, we will do more to help the lower-income groups with their public transport fares.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We had earlier disbursed Public Transport Vouchers, or PTVs, to every household that received a PTV in the last exercise and that includes over 30,000 ComCare beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will do another round of disbursements this month for these ComCare recipients.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they will receive $60 of PTVs, which will roughly cover the additional fares paid by a family of four this year arising from the fare increase last December.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides these ComCare recipients, PTVs are also available to all households whose monthly income per member does not exceed $1,600.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Applications for PTVs are open from now to 31 October this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Eligible households which had already received the first voucher and who need a second voucher can also apply again.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Lower-income persons with disabilities who require point-to-point services to commute can also apply for the Taxi Subsidy Scheme, which covers up to 80% of the taxi fares that they pay going to school, work or training.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This cushions them from the impact of recent fare surcharges introduced by taxi and ride-hailing app operators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me respond to the queries raised by several Members on fuel duties and road tax rebates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We collect fuel duties and road taxes for revenue and also to price the negative externalities of vehicle transport, such as the impact on public health and the environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Fuel duties collected averaged $920 million a year over the last five years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The revenue from these duties and taxes adds to the pool of resources available for various programmes and subsidies that directly benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These include spending on public transport, for which we provide significant capital investments, as well as operating subsidies to ensure an affordable and world-class public transport system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Given the recent increase in pump prices, I can understand why some Members have asked to reduce or suspend fuel duties, or to provide road tax rebates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But doing so effectively amounts to a subsidy on private transport and will have counter-productive effects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Fewer than four in 10 households in Singapore own cars and, amongst the lowest quintile, only about one in 10 do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Four in 10 is the overall but, if you look at the lowest quintile, the bottom 20% of households by income, only one in 10 owns cars.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Such subsidies on private transport would, therefore, benefit a relatively small but generally better-off group.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Cutting fuel duties also means that some of the subsidies will flow back, in part, to producers and suppliers themselves, not just to consumers, as the pump price may not fall as much as the reduction in duty.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More importantly, such subsidies will reduce the incentive to switch to more energy-efficient modes of transport, which is a critical element in our plans for sustainable living.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I recognise that there are several groups like taxi and private hire car drivers and delivery riders, who are affected by the increases in petrol and diesel prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Various taxi and private hire car operators have implemented temporary increases in fares to help cushion the higher fuel prices for drivers and to have consumers share the burden.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They also have tie-ups with petrol companies to offer fuel at discounted prices to help drivers and riders manage higher fuel costs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as I mentioned earlier, those whose incomes are impacted and are in need of financial assistance can approach the SSOs, CCs or self-help groups for more help.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Overall, the better way to help Singaporeans cope with the rise in petrol prices, as with inflation in general, is to provide them with the support measures that we have catered for in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to monitor the external situation and the risks for our economy closely – risks, both in terms of growth and inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And where inflation is concerned, we are monitoring this closely, not just the headline figure but also the impact of inflation on different income groups and even the issue of shrinkflation, which Ms He Ting Ru asked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But even without the war, we would, eventually, have to adjust to a secular increase in energy prices, as we seek to decarbonise our economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Likewise, on the manpower front, we will continue to face a tight labour market, given our rapidly-ageing population.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, a better approach, a more viable approach is to redouble our economic restructuring and transformation efforts, to become more innovative, productive and energy-efficient.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These efforts will help our economy become more resilient to external shocks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is also how we sustain continued income growth for Singaporeans, with earnings rising faster than inflation, so that we can retain and grow our purchasing power and achieve higher standards of living.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Sometimes, it does take a crisis to jolt all of us into action because, for many years, to illustrate, the Government had highlighted the importance of digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But take-up rates for digitalisation schemes were uneven.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, when COVID-19 struck, businesses had to adjust quickly and, within two years, we managed to achieve much more in our digitalisation efforts than all the combined efforts over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the same way, I hope that the current increase in business costs and energy prices will motivate firms to change their mindsets, processes and practices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government has put in place many schemes in this Budget and in previous Budgets, to help companies improve their productivity and energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And Minister Tan See Leng will elaborate further on them later.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I urge businesses to make full use of this support and to accelerate their restructuring and transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Doing so will strengthen their abilities to withstand shocks and position them well for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These events underscored our vulnerabilities to inflation, as a price-taking small and open economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, in response, in the early 1980s, we developed a unique exchange rate-centred monetary policy that helped tame imported inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Labour Movement played a vital role in stabilising prices with the establishment of NTUC Welcome, which evolved to become the NTUC FairPrice of today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By buying essentials like rice in bulk and passing on the savings to consumers, NTUC not only tackled profiteering among wholesalers, but also helped workers and Singaporeans beat inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: NTUC FairPrice continues to help mitigate cost of living pressures through various initiatives and discount schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis, we acted quickly to save jobs amidst a global recession, implementing the Jobs Credit Scheme, the precursor to our more recent Jobs Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As a result of this and other interventions, our economy rebounded swiftly in 2010.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, all of these crises paled in comparison to the COVID-19 pandemic and also our worst recession, since Independence, in 2020.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our swift and decisive action to protect lives and livelihoods enabled resident employment and incomes to quickly recover to pre-COVID-19 levels by 2021 while keeping COVID-19 deaths low.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now, before we have had the chance to see through the pandemic, we are faced with yet another economic challenge.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After many years of relative price stability, the recent surge of inflation has, understandably, come as a shock to many.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But when viewed against the global context and our own experience, I hope we can better understand the causes of higher prices and what we can do to manage this together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must not let this become a blame game of Government versus people, of sellers versus buyers, of hawkers versus consumers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Or worse, think that if Singapore were to lie low and remain silent on the war in Ukraine, we could somehow all enjoy lower pump prices today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What we are experiencing today in Singapore is the result of external forces that impact the entire global economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We cannot do very much to change this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But what we can do is to continue to keep faith with one another, as we have done over the last two years – look out for one another, help those in need and never waver from the conviction that we will always have one another's backs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If the situation worsens and more support is needed, the Government stands ready to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we will get through this together, as we have always done, as one united people.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Tan See Leng will be making a related Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will allow Members to raise points of clarifications on both Statements after this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong has given Members an overview of the macroeconomic environment, the outlook for inflation and the support for households.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we work to manage the immediate cost pressures that businesses and households are facing, it is equally important that we strengthen our economic resilience and prepare ourselves for a possibly protracted uncertain operating environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will also address Members' questions on support for businesses and on profiteering.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Domestically, around 95% of our electricity is generated from imported natural gas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our electricity generation companies (gencos), generally, rely on long-term Piped Natural Gas (PNG) and Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) contracts to meet their needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They use spot LNG, on an opportunistic basis, to supplement their long-term contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By and large, this has allowed us to keep electricity prices relatively stable and mitigate the impact of global price shocks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, we cannot fully insulate ourselves from the volatilities in the global energy market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since September last year, a confluence of factors has caused the prices of oil and natural gas to spike, and this has spilled over into our domestic energy market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Increased oil and gas consumption as major economies around the world emerged from the pandemic, seasonally-high energy consumption during the winter months in the northern hemisphere and a series of unexpected gas production outages led to a supply-demand mismatch in global energy markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Closer to home, upstream production issues in Indonesia's West Natuna gas field and gas pressure issues from South Sumatra in the fourth quarter of 2021 caused disruptions to our PNG supplies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As a result, some gencos had to purchase more spot LNG at elevated global gas prices to make up for the drop in PNG supplies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Although some of the demand pressures have abated as winter in the northern hemisphere comes to an end and upstream gas production issues in Indonesian gas fields have been resolved, the gas supply situation continues to remain tight and this is exacerbated and made protracted by the conflict in Ukraine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As I have shared with the House previously, MTI and EMA have put in place measures to secure our electricity supply and maintain the orderly functioning of the wider energy sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also put in place requirements for gencos to contract sufficient fuel to meet their commitment to customers' demands and needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These measures bolster our gencos' existing stockpile and they provide additional layers of fuel security to cope with the short-term shocks to global gas supply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, they are costly and will need to be carefully calibrated to manage the cost impact on consumers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, to maintain power system stability and reliability, we modified market rules to allow EMA to direct gencos to generate electricity using gas from the SLF, if there are potential temporary shortages in energy supply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These measures have ensured that we have sufficient fuel and electricity supply and stabilised the Uniform Singapore Energy Price (USEP).

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is compared to an average of $460 per MWh in the fourth quarter of last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since January 2022, EMA has also been working with electricity retailers and gencos to help large consumers to secure retail contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, businesses can secure one-month fixed price plans and retail contracts with significant fixed price components through the Temporary Electricity Contracting Support Scheme (TRECS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So far, there has been sufficient supply under TRECS to meet demand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA has also worked with Sembcorp Power and Keppel Electric to offer long-term fixed price plans for business consumers with an average monthly consumption ranging from four MWh to 50 MWh.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These plans range from six months to three years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA's efforts ensure that consumers, especially those affected by exiting retailers, can choose from a range of retail contracts to suit their needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Such longer-term contracts also provide gencos with more certainty of demand, which allow them to contract for the gas that is needed to serve consumers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will give businesses, especially SMEs, a bit more time to respond to the evolving global energy situation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA will continue to monitor the situation and consider extending the measures further or introduce new measures, if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But as consumers, we must also be prepared mentally to face higher electricity bills over time, especially if the price of oil and gas remains elevated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government can and will help to smooth out extreme fluctuations in energy prices, but, over the longer-term, electricity prices will have to reflect the costs of procurement and production.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is not tenable for the Government to subsidise electricity consumption in Singapore, in order to keep domestic electricity prices lower than the global prices which Singapore must pay for energy in the first place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Those on retail contracts have already started to see higher electricity prices when renewing their contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These higher electricity prices reflect the increasing costs of electricity production in this challenging climate and may continue to increase, depending on the direction of fuel price movements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The protracted energy crunch has highlighted the need to make our power system more resilient and less susceptible to fuel supply shocks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since 2014, we have sought to diversify our fuel sources to safeguard our energy security by building an LNG terminal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows us to tap on gas sources further afield.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The LNG terminal has sufficient capacity to meet all our natural gas needs should PNG be unavailable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government has taken the lead in accelerating rooftop solar deployment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One example is the SolarNova programme, which aggregates demand for solar systems across the public sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Besides decarbonising the power sector, this will also reduce our reliance on natural gas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond this, we will continue to explore other low-carbon alternatives, such as hydrogen, geothermal and, as what Minister of State Alvin Tan alluded to earlier on, even nuclear energy, which may have the potential to improve our energy security and our energy resilience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These measures will take time to bear fruit, but we will have a more secure and resilient power system over time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Minister for Finance has touched on the Government's efforts to help households defray utilities costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Each of us, as fellow Singaporeans, can also do our part.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I urge all of us to conserve energy, just like how we conserve water.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Small lifestyle adjustments, such as switching off appliances when they are not in use, raising the temperatures in an air-conditioned environment by one to two degrees and using the fan instead of air-conditioning where possible, can go a long way in maintaining a sustainable, secure and resilient energy future for all of us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As the Minister for Finance mentioned, the Government is closely monitoring food prices and will continue to ensure that basic food necessities remain accessible and affordable for everyone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are also keeping a close watch on global supply chains and our stock levels of essential food items to ensure that Singapore continues to have access to adequate supplies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Thankfully, our supply of essential food products has not been significantly affected by the Ukraine-Russia conflict and we have not had to draw on our food stockpiles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we will continue to diversify our import sources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will ramp up our stockpiles and supplies from alternative sources, where needed, to ensure that we have continued access to basic food necessities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I would also like to assure the House that we have put in place measures to ensure that we have adequate fuel supplies, including petroleum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members will appreciate that it would not be appropriate for me to share the specifics of this plan for security reasons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, pump operators have raised petrol and diesel prices to reflect the rise in crude oil prices over the past months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some landlords have also passed on increased utility costs to their tenants, including those in food courts and coffee shops.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Code of Conduct for Leasing of Retail Premises, which was issued by the Fair Tenancy Industry Committee (FTIC) last year, sets out guidelines on how landlords can do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Often, these increases are understandable as businesses are also facing pressure on their bottom-lines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But, there are also many other businesses that have gone out of their way to hold prices steady and offer discounts to consumers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These comprise household staples, such as rice, oil, eggs, milk and vegetables, and they should help to mitigate some of the cost pressures felt by households.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Giant has also committed to keeping the prices of essential items stable and recently expanded coverage to include close to 150 essential products.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some Members have also expressed concern about profiteering behaviour.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS) keeps a close watch on the movements in pump prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So far, movements in pump prices largely mirror the movements in crude oil prices, though they have increased to a smaller extent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have no evidence to suggest that there is collusion amongst the petrol retailers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: CCCS will take firm enforcement action, including imposing financial penalties, on infringing firms, if there is any evidence of anti-competitive behaviour, such as coordinated price increases, and this applies across the board to any industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To deter unreasonable pricing, we will also support consumers in being well-informed on alternative options.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Price Kaki application and the Fuel Kaki website developed by the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) allow consumers to easily compare the effective prices of groceries, hawker food items and retail pump prices across different retailers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will help consumers make better purchasing decisions where retailers choose to maintain prices but reduce the quantity of products.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Committee Against Profiteering (CAP) has also been reconvened ahead of the GST increase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The role of CAP is to investigate feedback on unjustified increases in the prices of essential products and services using the GST increase as an excuse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: CAP Chairman Minister of State Low Yen Ling has shared that the work of the Committee is more complex due to the current inflationary climate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nevertheless, CAP will review and evaluate all the feedback it receives and engage businesses where necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: CAP may name and shame businesses that use the GST increase as an excuse to raise prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Such behaviour artificially inflates costs to households and businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will work closely with our industry partners to diversify our supply chains, investigate anti-competitive behaviour, encourage price transparency and enable free market competition to function as it should.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ultimately, this is the best way to safeguard all of our consumer interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members have asked what the Government can do to help businesses and households cope with the rising costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we must also be prepared for longer-term trends that may put further upward pressure on prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Minister for Finance has touched on some of these trends in his speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we will work with a range of stakeholders to carefully manage the various cost drivers faced in the near term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOF has touched on measures to help households manage the higher costs of living.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government has also set aside considerable resources to help businesses, especially SMEs, cope with higher costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Grant will help eligible firms in sectors most badly affected by COVID-19 restrictions and is also available to SFA-licensed operators and stallholders in markets, hawker centres, coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: IRAS will notify businesses of their eligibility and disburse the grant from June this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The $500 million Jobs and Business Support Package, including the extended Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI), will support firms with their investments in workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Progressive Wage Credit Scheme will also support businesses with their manpower costs as they uplift the wages of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Minister for Finance announced a $2 billion injection into this scheme at Budget this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The extension of enhanced enterprise loan schemes will facilitate SMEs’ continued access to financing and ease their cashflow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These measures were announced at Budget just last month and it reflects our commitment to supporting our businesses through this difficult period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are closely monitoring the situation and will provide more support for affected sectors, if needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As electricity prices rise, being energy-efficient will become increasingly important to managing business costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have already put in place several measures to help businesses improve their energy efficiency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, NEA's Energy Efficiency Fund provides grants for manufacturing companies to adopt energy-efficient technologies; BCA's Green Mark Incentive Scheme provides grants for building owners to improve the energy performance of existing buildings; and ESG's Enterprise Sustainability Programme supports local enterprises to optimise energy and carbon use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We understand that more businesses will be looking at ways to improve their energy efficiency and make their operations greener and more sustainable during this period.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will do its part to assist companies in this transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are studying various options, such as expanding the range of supportable solutions or making it easier for businesses to apply for existing grants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Fuel intensive sectors, such as transport and logistics, have also been hard hit by volatile petrol prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We encourage our firms to double down on operating more efficiently and sustainably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes taking part in industry initiatives to share jobs to optimise asset utilisation, to use fleet management systems to track and monitor fuel consumption.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By being more resource-efficient, businesses can better deal with unexpected, exogenous shocks that come our way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It goes a long way to improving our resilience and our energy security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will continue to work with industries and firms to transform and improve their overall productivity, so as to sustain real wage growth for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: PSG supports companies as they adopt various solutions to improve their productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also expanded the coverage of the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit (SFEC) to allow more smaller and micro enterprises to benefit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOF has also announced a new $70 million grant to be administered by NTUC to support companies with Company Training Committees (CTCs) to implement their transformation plan, redesign jobs and upskill workers for better workforce productivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I urge all of our firms that there is no better time than now to tap on these resources, adapt, transform and better position themselves for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As a small country, we cannot close ourselves off from the rest of the world just to avoid importing inflation or exposing ourselves to the volatilities in the global markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Two, even when prices do go up, we will do our best to cushion the impact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Fourth, last but not least, we will continue to monitor, watch the situation closely and consider providing further assistance, if needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The past two years have, indeed, been challenging for all of us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many businesses have been looking forward to riding the wave of a strong recovery in the global economy as we emerge from this pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Ukraine conflict and global inflationary pressures add considerable volatility and stress to what is an already challenging business environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But let us not be pessimistic about the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will need, together as a nation, to strengthen our defences against external shocks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will need to continue to pivot, transform our businesses to adapt to the changing global environment and we have done this many times before.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Above all, we will need to work together – the people, businesses and the Government – so that we can weather the headwinds and emerge stronger.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I would just like to understand with regard to the extension of the financial support for short- and medium-term assistance that Minister Lawrence Wong talked about earlier.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Since the Government is already prepared to provide this extension of support – and I think we can safely be assured that the lowest income amongst us will be hit by the inflationary pressures and we all understand that beyond the actual pain of having to pay more are the anxiety, frustration and uncertainty that could hurt us more, presenting vulnerabilities for people to exploit in our society – what are the downsides of just making this three-month extension to our lowest-income automatic?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One, for Finance Minister Lawrence Wong, is in relation to the Parliamentary Question which I had in terms of the fuel excise duties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Does the $900-plus million that was mentioned relate to all petroleum products or is it only for petrol and diesel which are sold to end-consumers at the pump, since we do have quite a substantial petrochemical industry as a whole?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second question is, again, in relation to fuel prices, but probably more for Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look at Brent crude prices, the last time, it was above US$100 a barrel was sometime in 2012 to 2014.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Back then, 95 Petrol was going at about $2.20 to $2.40.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But, today, when Brent is above US$100 again, people see that the pump prices are now about $3.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, can the Minister share the structural factors that actually contributed to these higher pump prices, just so that everyone can have a better sense of what are the contributing factors to these 20% to 40% higher pump prices relative to Brent crude prices?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I shared earlier on, we have been monitoring in terms of the fluctuation of the prices against Brent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We find that it has not gone up excessively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think that it is like "apple to apple" comparison between what has happened, I think, in 2014, the target grade and what it is today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because, obviously, other fixed costs would have gone up – rental, perhaps – also manpower cost, plus it could be even different types of production or procurement costs that are not just tied to Brent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I think that it would be a lot more precise to compare what was the prevailing quarter and the movements, and to see whether that increase is actually attributable to whether it is signaling or collusion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that would give us a much better indication.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, when the hon Deputy Prime Minister announced the hike in petrol tax in February 2021, he pegged the reasons for increasing it as to promote a green environment, not revenue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, at the time when he announced the tax hike, the Ukraine invasion would not have been foreseeable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But at that point in time, he and the Government officers would have calibrated a certain behaviour pattern in terms of an increase in the fuel price and how much behaviour would have changed from that point onwards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, since the announcement was made, the price was hiked by about 10%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, we all accept that the war drove up the price.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, since 24 February 2022, when the invasion happened, to date, the price at the pumps has increased about 5%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, why could we not calibrate downwards the fuel tax so that we have an optimal behaviour that was planned as at February 2021?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second question is: if the Minister still does not intend to intervene, then when does he think is a proper time to intervene, having regard to the fact that a number of vehicles are used by fellow Singaporeans for their trades and businesses?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We collect fuel duties for both revenue as well as externality reasons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The revenues generated are not small and they are used for a range of very important things, to subsidise many activities: public transport, whole range of things, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, four in 10 is the average.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in the end, the ones who benefit more are the better-off when you do something like that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, is that the best use of subsidies?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thirdly, we will be moving in the wrong direction because fuel duties price in the negative externalities, as we all understand, to society and to the environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In a way, you can think of them akin, in part, to a carbon tax on vehicles, because we do not apply carbon tax on fuel.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Fuel duties are akin, in part, to carbon tax on vehicles.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are already moving on carbon tax: to raise carbon tax, to accelerate our green transition and to achieve our net-zero target.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will not be consistent as we move on that front to, on the other hand, reduce fuel duties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why, on balance, we think the better approach is not to intervene in this way.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are saying we will help people who are affected, we will continue to help them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have been helping and we will continue to monitor the situation and, for those who need more help and if the situation worsens, we will certainly do more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the better way of helping is not through a reduction in fuel duties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The better way of helping is to directly help those who are impacted through other means and we have these different means to help those who are impacted, be it households or businesses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With this new development, could the Government consider a special additional tranche of U-Save rebates to help Singaporeans cope with this upcoming electricity hike?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, now in this handout, the January 2023 U-Save rebate is listed as part of the support for households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, can I clarify that the January 2023 U-Save rebate is now part of the HSP and not the AP and, if so, should not there be an additional U-Save rebate for the AP?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, I just want to clarify, the Second Minister, I think, did not answer my question about whether the Committee Against Profiteering (CAP) will address concerns that businesses could use reasons other than the rise in GST as a pretext to make unjustified price increases on essential products and services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you listen to the Budget speech, we highlighted the concerns that Singaporeans had about higher prices then.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Prices had already increased because of the tensions in Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We put in place a HSP of $560 million that will be disbursed this year and we enhanced the AP.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, in fact, we have sized the AP very generously.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now, for GST-offset purposes, five years is very generous.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We could have said "two to three years of offsets are more than enough", but we sized it deliberately, generously, in order to cushion the impact on Singaporeans, especially the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why when you combine the HSP and AP together, there is considerable support that will be going out very soon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Every quarter, there will be another $150, so, $600 altogether.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is enough to cover about four months' worth of their utility bills, even accounting for higher electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now, you say: well, what happens, subsequently, in the next half of the year?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What if oil prices go up much higher, electricity prices go up much higher?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, we will, as I have said, continue to monitor the situation, assess the impact of what we have already announced and will implement, looking at the global situation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, as I have said just now, if the situation worsens, the Government will do more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, earlier on in my speech, I also alluded to the fact that we have got apps, like Price Kaki, Fuel Kaki – and these are developed by CASE – to allow consumers to easily compare the prices of groceries or hawker food items from different sellers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, CAP will also work with various agencies and organisations, including the Competition Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS), CASE and People's Association (PA), to assess the feedback provided on potential GST profiteering.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: CAP will also engage with the relevant businesses, where necessary, to find out the reasons for these price increases.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, today, we have convened CAP ahead of the proposed GST increase to make sure that we are able to pre-empt some of these things.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think it is also an important point – CAP will, indeed, take a data-driven approach to prioritise its investigations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, just to put it in perspective, perhaps for the Member's clarity, CCCS monitors market concentration data and shares this data with CAP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Then, CAP will review all feedback provided on unjustified price increases which use GST increase as a cover and investigate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that that provides the clarity that is needed to the Member's question.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I appreciate the Finance Minister's considerations for not cutting duties on petrol, chief amongst these considerations being that it subsidises private transport, which the less well-off may consume less of.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But diesel undergirds so much of our supply chain and, indeed, the delivery of essential goods and services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And that is the reason why I filed a question specifically on the possibility of cutting the duty on diesel products.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I just hope to seek a clarification from the Finance Minister as to the possibility of this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And then now, at the first sign of price rising, we are wanting to withdraw so quickly?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I think let us have some perspective on seeing the broader considerations and challenges.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, we have, indeed, an immediate issue of inflation to tackle.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we also want to press ahead with our net-zero plans and our green transition.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These duties are there for that purpose, an important purpose.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It does not mean we will not do anything to help the affected groups at all, because we will find other ways to help.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will continue to monitor the well-being, not just of households, but of the different groups that Members have highlighted: taxi drivers, private hire car drivers, delivery drivers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to monitor closely their incomes, their well-being and, if need be, as I highlighted just now, we will do more to help them, but we will help them directly, more effectively, rather than through a reduction in duties.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Can I know who actually decides on a price hike of electricity prices?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Is it the Government, EMA or SP Group?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am stating this as a concern because I am also an employee of SP Group.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Whenever there is a price hike that is being mentioned, my fellow members and workers at the workplace and facing the public will always be asked, "How come you have a price hike?" So, I hope, if that challenge can be left to EMA to announce the price hike, compared to SP Group, that would actually help to eliminate the stress that is faced by my fellow members and workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think there is a confluence of the sector agencies that determine the price hike.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, PSP is of the view that inflation is here to stay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The earlier and the more contingency plans we have, the better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So far, all our discussion in this Chamber has concentrated on cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two questions to ask the Minister for Manpower about income and wages.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, because Singaporeans are in constant competition with foreigners, how to ensure Singaporean workers will continue to be competitive vis-a-vis foreign manpower in a rising wage environment?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have been very focused on uplifting the lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, I think the whole crux of this year's Committee of Supply (COS) and pretty much the last two quarters of last year, Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad has gone out to talk about the Progressive Wage Model, how we have set up schemes, we have also illustrated the fact that the bottom 20%, in terms of their wage growth over the years, has exceeded the median wage rise for the rest of the salaries in our constant and consistent efforts to ensure that we continue to uplift our low-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is one big portion of what uplifting is all about.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the Member had sat through the MOM COS, our three focuses this year were uplifting, upgrading and upholding.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, while we uplift them, we also have to upgrade them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the significant programmes in terms of upskilling them, reskilling, helping them to pivot, we have, together, on a multi-sectoral, multi-Ministerial level, gotten the industry transformation maps and to match the industry transformation maps with the Job Transformation Map (JTM) which provides a very good guide and compass as to where companies are, in terms of the development forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have Productivity Solutions Grant, multiple different schemes to help companies to pivot while we train and upgrade our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We ensure that with the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness (TCWF), we are now looking at how we are going to move this into legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, for foreign workforce complementarity, we have also rolled out COMPASS, which is a complementarity assessment framework to allow us to bring in foreign talent in a very nuanced way so that they are able to contribute to our strategic economic priorities, they can address the training of our locals in uplifting and making sure that we are world-class in terms of our workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those are a whole multitude of measures that we have put in place.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Obviously, we are also working in terms of making sure that we strengthen the retirement savings in our CPF account, we continue to press ahead, to nudge our people to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The entire list of measures that we have done to help our local Singaporeans continue to move ahead, to make sure that their real wages exceed inflationary rates, I think those are the measures that we have.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am not sure what other suggestions or other better solutions PSP has today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Just to confirm what the Minister has said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the Progressive Wage Credit has taken into consideration future rise in inflation to ensure that Singaporeans' incomes and wages rise with inflation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If he would like to file a separate Parliamentary Question on the manpower issues, I am happy and always waiting for him to do so.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, the big question is, how high, what is the threshold that you are waiting for before more help can be delivered and what is the help that the businesses and the citizens can expect?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We look at our economic growth, for example.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But what we can do is continue to work hard on all the things we are doing to restructure, transform the economy, uplift productivity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those efforts will pay off and will help us year by year to ensure that incomes rise and, hopefully, continue to rise faster than inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You cannot dictate wages, but you can continue to press ahead with restructuring and transformation, which is what we are doing across all our economic agencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the point of how high should inflation have to be before we see more help, I think that is what Dr Lim Wee Kiak is asking.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am not able to give a specific trigger point now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said, we will monitor a range of indicators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Not just the headline of economic growth, inflation, for that matter, unemployment, but also how it impacts different groups and different income groups, different occupations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And then, what is the impact of our current package of measures which has not been implemented?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We need to see that properly implemented and feed through the economy as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the past Meet-the-People sessions online, there were a few residents who are local small SMEs who came to me highlighting about the rise in electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I think it is in reference to my Parliamentary Question as well on small SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my question is, with regard to whether MTI or MOF is amenable to a lower-tier TRECS, for example, as we know, the TRECS that we have now is applied to larger SMEs and whether, in the future, there could be a lower tier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is, local SMEs are very important because they employ quite a significant number of workers and we are talking about wages, jobs and unemployment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to address the local SMEs which employ a significant number of our local workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And such a move, if it is amenable to MTI or MOF, in terms of a lower-tier TRECS in the future, whether that is a possibility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think when you look at the tier, indeed, this is exactly what we have tried our level best to do.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, for companies, SMEs or even larger enterprises which do not want to go on a fixed price contract for a longer term, we offer them TRECS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is on a monthly basis because there are many SMEs that are still hoping that the current high prices are temporary and they are hoping that, with the spot prices, thinking that by the time they reach June or July, they may drop.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, they want to hold off and wait for it to drop before they enter into a longer-term contract.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, to the extent that is possible, what we have done is that we have continued to ensure stability, security, consistency of the supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The pricing part, what we have tried to do is also to negotiate on their behalf to see how, depending on the needs of the different companies, some, because they feel they cannot take a long-term hedge, we then provide on a monthly basis and that is TRECS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For those companies which feel that they need to have this at least on a stable basis for six months, we have also provided the option for that and then up to a year, two years and three years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that, today, is a very nuanced approach that we have adopted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could I clarify with Minister Lawrence Wong that there will actually be no specific measures that are targeted towards households as well as small businesses that are operating in the transportation sector?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, I understand Minister Lawrence Wong's arguments about how broad-based fuel excise taxes are regressive and, of course, I understand the concept – I would like to think I understand the concept – of externalities and I also wish that these Budget measures, when they are brought forward, should be allowed to operate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, CPI was 4.3% but it was 17.2% in the latest figures for the transportation sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, households operating vehicles for commercial purposes, while they do benefit from budgetary measures as consumers, they are also facing higher prices as both consumers and producers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, even if you wish to limit the beneficiaries of transportation-specific relief, I wonder whether there will be some targeted measures either captured by the road taxes that are being paid by these families or in terms of whether they use commercial vehicles for the purposes of business.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I mentioned just now, some companies are already making adjustments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are already raising their fares to help their drivers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, some taxi companies are still continuing with rental concessions and there are other companies that are also doing other things to help their delivery drivers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are in place today, which means that the costs are being shared with consumers because the fares go up, delivery rates go up, which means that the costs are shared in part, not just borne solely by these delivery riders but shared with consumers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They would be eligible if they meet the criteria.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, the COVID-19-related situation, the supply chain stressors, the war in Ukraine and the wages in which we want to have wage uplift.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, my concern is that there is this series of cost increases and price increases, it will inter-feed into each other and whether that will trigger off an inflationary spiral.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Finance Minister what can the Government do to break this chain of interaction in the prices and the costs and then to counter this momentum of price increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is for Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I appreciate the Committee Against Profiteering (CAP) to check on unjustifiable profiteering.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we also know that this is not a magic bullet.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: You still need competition to counter all these profiteering and there must be choices for consumers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask Minister Tan See Leng whether CAP would focus more on those sectors or businesses that have less choices for consumers, less competition where their businesses have bigger market power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How can we focus on those and, in particular, whether CAP or CCCS has identified any of these sectors?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I said Small Business Recovery Grant is extended to different sectors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is for the sectors affected most by SMMs, which mostly are F&B and retail.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the broader point remains, which is, that many of these companies in the transport and logistics sector have made arrangements, fares are going up, they are cost sharing with consumers, who also benefit through the help measures from the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us monitor what is happening in this space, the effects of our measures, before we consider next steps.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as far as the labour market tightness is concerned, there are some ways in which we can help ease the current situation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, do not take it for granted that the Government has all the money to do everything because we also have to ensure sound and sustainable public finances at the end of the day.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Tan See Leng, can you wrap up?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Sorry, Mr Speaker, because Mr Liang Eng Hwa had two questions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier on, I had shared that we will also take a data-driven approach to prioritise the investigations and I said that there will be a sharing of data across different agencies itself.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think one thing I want to thank the Member for suggesting is the observation, in terms of some of those very small sort of tight sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the best way to counter profiteering is really to promote competition, to have a wider range of service and product offerings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, those are things that we are indeed looking into.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: End of Ministerial Statement on Inflation and Business Costs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Now, we will proceed to the Ministerial Statement by the Minister for Law, Mr Shanmugam.
